definition: The use of crowdsourcing and text corpus in human-machine translation (HMT) within the last few years have become predominant in their area, in comparison to solely using machine translation (MT).
details: There have been a few recent academic journals looking into the benefits that using crowdsourcing as a translation technique could bring to the current approach to the task and how it could help improve and make more efficient the current tools available to the public.

explainer.lead: Crowdsourcing in human-machine translation combines contributions from many people with machine translation and text corpora, rather than relying on machine translation alone. It is being studied as a way to improve translation and make publicly available tools more efficient.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a computer translating a sentence, then lots of people helping with the tricky words and phrases. They can also look at collections of existing writing to see how words are usually used. Together, the people and computer can produce a translation without either having to do all the work alone.
tiers.practitioner: In an HMT workflow, machine translation can provide a draft while corpus evidence and crowd contributions help resolve or revise it. Design decisions include what contributors see, how their submissions are combined, and how the result is reviewed. More contributions do not automatically remove problems with ambiguous text or inconsistent translations.
tiers.paperLevel: The setup can be written as HMT = f(MT output, corpus evidence, crowd contributions), where f denotes their combination into a translation. The research question is whether adding distributed human work improves translation and tool efficiency relative to using MT alone.

explainer.example: For the English sentence “I sat by the bank,” a machine produces a draft French translation. Crowd contributors use the sentence context and corpus examples to support “rive” rather than “banque,” and the reviewed choice becomes the final HMT output.

usedIn.name: Human-machine translation
usedIn.detail: Crowd contributions, machine translation, and text corpora are combined in the translation process.

usedIn.name: Public translation tools
usedIn.detail: Crowdsourcing is being investigated as a way to improve available tools and make them more efficient.

explainer.intuition: Machines can supply a draft translation, while a crowd contributes human knowledge about wording and context. Text corpora provide additional examples of language use, so the process draws on several kinds of evidence instead of MT output alone.
howItWorks: Provide the source text to the human-machine translation workflow.
Let crowd contributors supply translations or revisions, informed by context and corpus examples.
Combine and review the contributions to produce the final translation.
explainer.whyItMatters: The approach brings distributed human effort into machine-assisted translation and offers a possible route to better, more efficient translation tools. Academic work has examined what benefits crowdsourcing could add to existing approaches.
misconceptions: It is not crowdsourcing alone: machine translation and text corpora remain part of the approach.
Adding more contributors does not by itself guarantee a better translation.

diagram.caption: Machine output and corpus evidence support crowd contributions, which feed into the reviewed translation.
